hero.title: Key Food Flavor Compounds Knowledge Base and Flavouring Regulation Lookup
hero.intro: Look up a food or a flavor compound: which compounds create a food's aroma, which foods a compound occurs in, and related research papers. Data are grouped into three tiers by strength of evidence.
legend.title: Evidence tiers
legend.t1k_desc: From the main text of the review by Dunkel et al. (2014): compounds confirmed by GC-O, quantitation and recombination experiments to contribute to the food's aroma.
legend.t1d_desc: From the FlavorDB database: the compound has been detected in the food. Detection does not mean it contributes to the aroma.
legend.t2_desc: Related papers retrieved live from Europe PMC when you open a page. Listed only, not summarized.
legend.t3_desc: Fetches the abstract for a DOI you enter and marks the flavor compound names it contains. Text matching only, not the paper's conclusions.

footer.data: Data: key food odorants quoted from the main text of Dunkel A, et al. Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2014, 53, 7124-7143 (doi:10.1002/anie.201309508) with page numbers; the full food by odorant matrix is in that article's Supporting Information. Detection data from FlavorDB2 (Garg N, et al. Nucleic Acids Res. 2018), CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; derived data on this site are shared under the same license. Compound names and structures from PubChem.
footer.apis: Literature services: Europe PMC and Crossref (free, no API key).
hero.sub: Key flavor compounds, detected compounds and papers, by food or compound.
footer.short: Key food odorants from Dunkel et al. 2014; detection data from FlavorDB2 (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, derived data shared alike); papers via Europe PMC and Crossref. See method & sources.
about.practice: To find the key flavor compounds of a food, I usually search the literature on Web of Science and PubMed, and check databases such as Flavornet and The Good Scents Company for odor, thresholds and roles in food. Detected does not mean key: GC-MS only shows that a compound is present, while a key flavor compound must actually contribute to the overall flavor, which is usually judged by combining OAV, ROAV, GC-O, and recombination and omission experiments. This is why this knowledge base labels key flavor compounds and detected compounds separately.
about.reg_what: The regulatory lookup page finds a flavouring's status in the EU, China and the US by name (Chinese or English), CAS number, FEMA number, FL number or GB 2760 code; the ingredient finder, the odor predictor and this knowledge base's substance cards show the same information.
about.reg_src_eu: EU: Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008, Annex I Part A, Table 1 (the Union list, introduced by Regulation (EU) No 872/2012), EUR-Lex consolidated version of 2026-02-16 (up to Commission Regulation (EU) 2026/175), checked 2026-10-21 with no later amending act. The consolidated version is a documentation tool; the Official Journal text is authentic. Commission content is reused under CC BY 4.0; this site extracts the FL numbers, CAS numbers, restrictions of use and footnotes, and summarises the restrictions. Substances in Annex III Part A (not to be added as such to food, e.g. coumarin) are noted separately.
about.reg_src_cn: China: GB 2760-2024 National Food Safety Standard for Uses of Food Additives (published 2024-02-08, in force 2025-02-08), tables B.2 (permitted natural flavourings) and B.3 (permitted synthetic flavourings), from the official text on the National Food Safety Standard database. Amendment No. 1 was still out for comment on 2026-10-21 and is not included. The site shows only whether a substance is listed, the table, code, FEMA number and Chinese name; the standard's text is not reproduced.
about.reg_src_us: US: 21 CFR Part 172 sections 172.510 (natural flavoring substances) and 172.515 (synthetic flavoring substances and adjuvants), Part 182 sections 182.10, 182.20, 182.40, 182.50 and 182.60 (GRAS spices, essential oils, extracts and synthetic flavorings), the Part 184 sections whose uses include flavoring, for substances that are flavourings themselves, and the flavour-related prohibitions of Part 189 (189.110 calamus, 189.113 cinnamyl anthranilate, 189.130 coumarin, 189.180 safrole; the other prohibitions are not flavourings and are not included), from the current eCFR text (up to date as of 2026-10-20, checked 2026-10-22). The eCFR is an unofficial editorial compilation, not an official legal edition of the CFR. The match of CAS numbers to sections, FEMA numbers and "no longer FEMA GRAS" notes come from the FDA list "Substances Added to Food" (updated 2026-09-08, checked 2026-10-22); FDA states that it is only a partial list and that information from non-FDA sources in it does not indicate FDA approval or evaluation. Both are US government works in the public domain. The site does not use the FEMA website or data published by FEMA.
about.reg_match_1: The regulatory lookup page includes all 2,475 entries of the EU Union list, the 15 substances in Annex III Part A, all 1,892 entries of GB 2760 tables B.2 and B.3, and 2,973 US entries: the 21 CFR flavouring sections, the flavour-related prohibitions of Part 189 and the substances with a FEMA number in the FDA list. Entries with the same CAS number are merged into one substance, 3,861 in all; 2,451 of them are in the site's molecule library (the ingredient finder's 5,072 molecules) and link to the ingredient finder, the odor predictor and the knowledge base. Entries without a CAS number are listed on their own, marked "No CAS number for this entry". The substance cards of the ingredient finder, the odor predictor and the knowledge base show the status of the site's molecules only (2,014 in the EU list, 1,283 in China's, 1,868 with US information, 2,386 in at least one). Library CAS numbers come from this knowledge base and PubChem.
about.reg_match_2: China's lists give no CAS numbers: FEMA numbers are matched to CAS through the US FDA "Substances Added to Food" inventory. For 30 synthetic flavourings with no usable FEMA number, the CAS number was verified in PubChem and supplemented by this site, and the page says so. English-name searches on the lookup page also use the English names in the GB 2760 tables and the FDA inventory names.
about.reg_match_us: US: 21 CFR gives no CAS numbers. CAS numbers are matched to sections through the FDA list's citations and then checked by name against the current eCFR text; where the FDA list cites a section but the name is not found in the current text, the eCFR prevails and only the FEMA number is shown, with a note. The 7 substances FDA removed from 172.515 in 2018 (83 FR 50490) are marked separately. "FEMA GRAS number in the FDA list" only reports what the FDA list says: FEMA GRAS is a self-determination by an industry association's expert panel (FEMA), not an FDA approval. The ingredient finder's "US" filter includes molecules in a 21 CFR flavouring section or with a FEMA number in the FDA list, and leaves out those prohibited by Part 189, removed in 2018 or no longer FEMA GRAS. FDA names are in capitals; the site shows them in ordinary case.
about.reg_match_3: The site's molecules do not distinguish stereoisomers. When a list entry is one configuration (e.g. d-, l-, cis, (E)-), the page adds a note; check that it is the same isomer.
about.reg_rule_1: "Not found in the list" only means the site found no match: a different CAS or FEMA number, no CAS number for the molecule, or a substance outside the site's library. It does not mean "not permitted".
about.reg_rule_2: Restrictions of use in the EU and China are one- or two-sentence summaries by this site; US 21 CFR limitations are quoted from the eCFR as written. The official text prevails. FEMA use levels are not shown.
about.reg_rule_3: There is no search by food category or conditions of use. In China, flavourings are used as needed for production, and some foods may not contain them (GB 2760 Annex B, table B.1).
about.reg_rule_4: For reference only; the latest official texts prevail. Not regulatory advice.
rq.sub: Check the regulatory status of a flavouring in the EU, China and the US.
rq.title: Flavouring regulatory lookup
rq.scope: Search by name (Chinese or English), CAS number, FEMA number, FL number or GB 2760 code. All 2,475 entries of the EU Union list (plus 15 substances in Annex III Part A), all 1,892 entries of GB 2760 tables B.2 and B.3 (B.2 388, B.3 1,504) and, for the US, the 21 CFR flavouring sections, the flavour-related prohibitions of Part 189 and the substances with a FEMA number in the FDA list (2,973 entries) are included, merged by CAS number into 3,861 substances, 2,451 of them in the site's molecule library.
rq.note: "Not found in the list" does not mean "not permitted": the CAS or FEMA number may simply not have matched. For reference only; the latest official texts prevail. Not regulatory advice.
rq.label: Name, CAS, FEMA, FL number or GB 2760 code
rq.count_more: {n} substances found; the first {k} are shown. Try a more specific query.
rq.none: "{q}" was not found in either list. Different spellings may not match; try a CAS number, FEMA number or code. Not found does not mean not permitted.
rq.footer: EU data: Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008, Annex I, EUR-Lex consolidated version of 2026-02-16, CC BY 4.0, extracted and summarised by this site. China: based on GB 2760-2024, no amendments included; official text on the National Food Safety Standard database. US: 21 CFR (eCFR, an unofficial compilation) and the FDA list "Substances Added to Food", public domain. See method & sources.
about.reg_practice: When looking for a substitute, regulation matters most after flavor. Checking the EU list, GB 2760 and 21 CFR one substance at a time used to take a long time; here the status in all three places can be looked up first to confirm that the candidates are on the permitted lists. This is only a first screen; the latest official texts prevail.
